Sphere Encapsulated Lunar Soil Seed Germination: A Comparative Study of Sodium Alginate Spherification 
Techniques as a Growth Media Substitute for Loose Lunar Regolith 
Ariel Litinski, Sophia Kissling, Marlee Marcelo, Ivanna Melnyk, Nidhi Padalkar 
Academy for Biotechnology, Morris County School of Technology 
Team Name: MCST Biotech 1 
Team ID: 25036 
Coach: Alessandro Pizzo 
April 12, 2026

Introduction 
Reliable agriculture and maintaining life on the Moon are proving to be extremely important in the 
advancement of space technology, particularly the ability to grow crops in media that are found in space, such 
as lunar regolith. Research interest was amplified further after 2022, when NASA announced successful plant 
growth in lunar regolith samples. This advancement inspired research determining which plants grow best in 
lunar regolith, as well as potential amendments to improve growth. Previously studied methods include seed 
coatings, pill capsules, and hydrogel blocks, among others, which have been researched and implemented 
countless times to help address issues with transporting seeds and maintaining them in harsh conditions; 
however, challenges in water and nutrient retention have remained prevalent. This experiment aims to explore 
new methods of replacing and carrying growth media for seeds, utilizing methods of spherification to control 
lunar dust, and allowing for greater water retention. Furthermore, it explores the growth of the nutrient-rich and 
fast-growing plant, Mizuna Mustard, in the harsh lunar regolith. Mizuna mustard grows within 2-3 months and 
is commonly used in small salads for a quick, nutrient-dense food source. Exploring the growth of mizuna 
mustard within a growth media substitute can help to identify if it has potential as a source of food for 
astronauts. 
 
Background 
Lunar regolith is composed of various materials, such as silicones and types of metals, such as iron and 
aluminum, but it has very few nutrients for vegetation to thrive in. Alternatively, it has been determined that 
growing plants in lunar regolith is possible, but due to its lack of vital nutrients, the incredibly coarse and rough 
texture, its poor water retention, and the lack of air circulation, growing vegetation is extremely difficult. 
(Wieger Wamelink, et. al., 2014) Along with these rough conditions, lunar regolith tends to stick together and 
form blocks of lunar soil when exposed to moisture from plant watering or environmental conditions. Many 
experiments aim to compare the lunar regolith with various growth substrates or to add materials to the lunar 
regolith to improve growth (e.g., fertilizers, coconut coir, and bacteria). With most of these experiments being 
successful in identifying potential improvements or contributing to research, the issue of water retention and 
sources of water to the plant are still prominent. To improve water retention, there have been various 
approaches, including hydrogels. Hydrogels allow for both nutrient and water retention. Indeed, these 
approaches do help, with the addition of nutrients and water retention, but the components of transportation, 
efficiency, and longevity for space still stand as a hole in research. This leads the focus to shift onto increasing 
water retention in harsh conditions, such as lunar soil, without sacrificing the need for sufficient nutrient 
amounts. Additionally, these approaches do not address the underlying issues with lunar regolith. Loose lunar 
regolith is also commonly known to damage equipment. It is a material that can be airborne easily, thus 
allowing it to separate from its pot/container, disrupting growth, and damaging surrounding equipment. 
However, spherification encapsulates these properties to prevent damage and dust mobility. It is able to contain 
the lunar regolith particles without allowing them to disperse since they are held in a membrane. In any case, 
watering plants in space also faces many obstacles, as the water separates from the plants without gravity. 
 
Not only are there issues with the transportation of soil and methods for watering, but the type of plant used 
within these experiments also plays a crucial role. It needs to be taken into consideration that the plant needs to 
be fast-growing and highly resilient to harsh conditions for efficacy when grown in space. It also needs to be 
nutrient-rich and easy to incorporate into various types of meals. An example of this type of crop would be any 
crop from the mustard family. Crops in the mustard family tend to be nutrient-dense, fast-growing, and also

resilient to harsh conditions. Mustard plants can begin growing within 15-30 days, and can be used as a simple 
green or incorporated into a mix of greens similar to a salad (Morsi et al., 2024). Mizuna Mustard’s tolerance to 
low-nutrient and low-water environments can be attributed to its shallow, but fibrous roots, which allow the 
plant to extract nutrients from topsoil levels and allow the plant to thrive in places where the environment is 
harsh. (Garrido-Ruiz, 2026) Experiments being done with Mizuna Mustard in space conditions helped to form a 
basis for how Mizuna Mustard grows in lunar soil. Research shows that Mizuna Mustard seeds can be reliable 
for 2-3 months. (Doughty, 2024). With this in mind, Mizuna is a key component of this experiment and is the 
optimal plant for the suggested growth setting. 
 
Additionally, transportation and early plant growth stages are two of the key components for growing healthy 
plants, an example of which is seed coatings. Some seed coatings have used polyacrylate, which is classified 
as a superabsorbent polymer or SAP, in order to retain water. (Amirkhani, et. al., 2023) Superabsorbent 
polymers allow for large amounts of water retention, which is extremely important in the case of harsh and 
infertile soil, such as lunar regolith, which is subject to rapid desiccation in low-humidity environments. It is 
important to maximize water retention to allow for the most efficient plant growth. Similar to hydrogels, these 
SAP polymers are used to increase water retention for crops. One of the most effective natural SAP polypers is 
sodium alginate. Sodium alginate has been largely recognized for its diverse usage, and when incorporated into 
soil or with various nutrients, it has been shown to improve plant growth in the early stages. Similar to sodium 
alginate as a seed coating, it can also be used as a coating to encapsulate nutrients to allow for early plant 
growth and health. 
 
Sodium alginate is often used in Direct and Reverse spherification, which is typically incorporated into food or 
drug delivery. Reverse spherification consists of submerging a liquid or paste containing calcium chloride(2%) 
into a bath with a 0.5% sodium alginate mixture, while Direct spherification consists of adding a paste of liquid 
containing 2% sodium alginate, dropped into a 0.5% calcium chloride bath. (Sen, 2017). Spherification is a 
method of utilizing sodium alginate and a calcium chloride or calcium lactate bath to form solid or 
liquid-centered sphere shapes. The sodium alginate, when in contact with the calcium chloride or lactate, forms 
a solid texture through the replacement of calcium ions. Reverse spherification involves using calcium chloride 
or calcium lactate and dropping it into a sodium alginate bath. On the contrary, Direct spherification consists of 
a sodium alginate solution being dropped into a calcium chloride or calcium lactate bath. With these processes, 
Reverse spherification forms a liquid center while Direct spherification results in a solid center. These methods 
have been applied in the pharmaceutical field, especially in drug delivery, to provide slow-release of medicines 
(Pet et al., 2025). Along with the release of nutrients, the outer coating also affects the membrane and sphere 
itself. A thicker membrane means a slower release of the material inside, while a thinner membrane will dictate 
a faster release of the material in the center. Thicker membranes also allow for longer water retention, which in 
turn allows more nutrient retention for the crops being grown. They have also been used in nutraceuticals for 
the delivery of turmeric (curcumin) supplements and have been seen to be effective as a delivery method 
(Jagtap, 2025). These benefits can be easily transferred to lunar regolith spheres. Instead of slowly releasing 
medicines, they slowly release fertilizer, preventing it from running out immediately and allowing it to be used 
over longer periods of time. Another major benefit of spherification is the ease with which it is handled due to 
the fact that the medicine or regolith is conveniently encapsulated. Small, free-floating particles are a major 
liability in zero gravity, but lunar regolith contained in a membrane is not able to disperse and damage or abrade 
equipment the same way loose regolith would.

Hypothesis 
The goal of this experiment is to demonstrate how a new method of growing plants in lunar regolith, Reverse 
and Direct spherification, can optimally support plant growth in terms of biomass, chlorophyll, nitrogen uptake, 
and overall plant length. Encapsulating the regolith will create a unique growth environment to combat the 
challenges posed by the lunar regolith. With the regolith encapsulated, it also indicates a slower release and 
movement of water, along with longer storage of nutrients. Foremost, regolith tends to form clumps (Jung et al., 
2025), and by forming even spheres of regolith, there will be consistent pore spaces. This is essential to plant 
growth and nutrient intake. Plants are unable to thrive then soil is compacted with no airspace. These pockets of 
space will give roots better access to oxygen, which is vital to their growth (Arablousabet & Povilaitis, 2024). 
Moreover, lunar regolith has extremely poor water retention, but the regolith spheres’ membrane will hold water 
in for longer periods of time, as shown through capillary action tests and spherification properties, and will also 
hold the moisture near the roots. Hence, the regolith spheres are more manageable for astronauts since it 
contains the regolith rather than allowing it to move freely and damage the equipment. 
Encapsulating the lunar regolith provides a unique opportunity to include other materials in the spheres. This 
experiment will include powder fertilizer containing Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium in a 14:14:14 ratio 
(Kratsch, 2010). Because of the previously mentioned benefits, plants grown in regolith spheres will 
demonstrate more growth and data that support harvesting after the 8-week growth period compared to plants 
grown in loose regolith with the same additives. Between Reverse and Direct spherification, Reverse 
spherification will likely be more effective because it tends to yield thicker and longer-lasting membranes. It is 
shown through the capillary action test that the Reverse spherification spheres, when dehydrated, will soak up 
the water better and rehydrate more quickly due to the thicker membrane. This, in turn, will allow for more 
water retention but also protect the roots of the plant as it grows out. This can be seen through the final results, 
with the final bubble structure, plant growth, nitrogen amounts, and chlorophyll. The group hypothesizes that if 
Reverse spherification of lunar regolith is used to transport mizuna mustard seeds, then the overall growth rate 
of the plants within that group will perform better because Reverse spherification will allow for a thicker, 
water-retaining membrane and slower nutrient release. 
 
Experimental Design & Controls 
The experiment includes two experimental groups and two control groups, negative and positive. The negative 
control group consisted of pots with loose lunar regolith and all materials used during the spherification process, 
but were kept loose and did not go through any spherification processes. This demonstrates whether the 
difference in growth was caused by the additives or the process of spherification. The positive control group 
consisted of pots with only conventional clay pellets to house and grow the seeds. Comparing the experimental 
sodium alginate spheres to clay pellets establishes a baseline to determine the spheres’ moisture-retention and 
nutrient-delivery capabilities compared to a widely accepted hydroponic growth medium (Sarrocco et al., 2004). 
The first experimental group contained one of the delivery methods for lunar regolith, created through sodium 
alginate spheres using Direct spherification. The second experimental group had the delivery method of lunar 
regolith, produced through sodium alginate spheres formed using Reverse spherification. As opposed to the 
gelled centers of the spheres made using Direct spherification, the spheres made using Reverse spherification 
have an ungelled liquid center, which is better suited for plant root and shoot expansion (Patel & Madhan, 
2021). There were two components for each of the two experimental groups: the mixture and the bath. The 
ingredients for these components stayed the same between groups, with the exception that sodium alginate was

used in the bath and calcium chloride was used in the bubble mixture to make spheres for the Direct 
spherification group, and vice versa for the Reverse spherification group. For preliminary testing, a capillary 
action test was done on dehydrated bubbles to test the water absorption and rehydration rates. This was done in 
a short period of time, where the spheres can be dehydrated, placed in a tube, and with added water at the 
bottom to test how the water spreads upwards. The results determine how the watering system will work in a 
zero-gravity environment. Since the experiment is testing the efficacy of a planting method rather than soil 
amendments, the loose regolith used in the negative control groups was amended with the same ingredients 
used to make the spheres for the experimental groups. 
 
All pots were grown in the same environment and area, without any variation. This area was inside a growth 
tent with the light intensity set to 230 μmol-m-2-s-1. The light intensity, however, was changed from 230 
μmol-m-2-s-1 to 148.5 μmol-m-2-s-1 at the start of week 4. There was also a watering schedule that watered each 
group for 5 minutes every 15 minutes using a water supply and a timed pump. There were 8 pots for each 
group, with the bottom-center tray containing two pots of the Direct spherification, Reverse spherification, and 
negative control groups. The Positive Control also ended up using one-third of an empty tray to fulfill the 
requirement of 8 pots per group. Additionally, each group, Negative Control, Positive Control, Direct, and 
Reverse, had its own tray of six pots. Each pot was 4.5 cm in height and width, with a base of 4 cm. Each pot 
was also 100 mL in volume, totaling to 800 mL of volume for each group. 
 
To ensure all pots get equal and adequate water throughout the 7 weeks, an ebb-and-flow hydroponic system 
was used. To assemble this system, the pots were placed on inverted plastic containers to sit above the water 
supply, which was poured into the large white tray and cleaned weekly. The ebb and flow system had a timed 
water pump, placed in the water supply, which turned on and flooded for 5 minutes and turned off for 15 
minutes while the water drained. This pump was connected to a tube separator, which sent 2 tubes to each of the 
6 trays. Small holes in the trays allowed for draining, while larger holes above them prevented overflooding. 
This system was cleaned, and the water was replaced every week 
 
Variables 
The independent variable was the method used to grow the seeds (Direct spherification spheres, Reverse 
spherification spheres, loose regolith, and clay pellets). The dependent variables included a variety of 
qualitative and quantitative measurements, with some taken throughout the growth period and others taken 
solely at the end of it. These measurements were plant height (with ImageJ, weekly), nutrient levels, leaf 
number (recorded weekly), final root length, final biomass, final plant length, and final leaf chlorophyll content. 
Materials 
The materials used for the creation and set up of lunar regolith spherification methods included: 36 100 mL pots 
(six count trays containing six pots each), 1872 g lunar regolith simulant, 79.68 g sodium alginate, 38.4 g 
calcium chloride, 3.456 g powdered 14-14-14 fertilizer, 14.4 g xanthan gum, 392.2 distilled water, 300 g clay 
pellets, 1 large white tray, 7 flexible plastic tubes, 1 tube separator, 1 water pump, 1 outlet timer, 1 growth tent 
with adjustable light settings. 
 
Procedure 
Control Groups:

To make the negative control group, a mixture of 624 g of lunar regolith simulant, 26.56 g of sodium alginate, 
12.8 g of calcium chloride, 4.8 g of xanthan gum, and 379.2 mL of water mixed with 1.152 g of powdered 
Osmocote Classic 14-14-14 fertilizer (Carolina Biological Supply) was created. A fertilizer ratio of 14-14-14 
(nitrogen to phosphorus to potassium) was selected over other ratios to ensure plants have equal access to 
nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Fertilizer was put into the spheres to supply seedlings with adequate 
nutrients and allow their roots to enter nearby spheres to access more nutrients (Shaviv, 2001). 100 mL of the 
mixture was added to each of 8 pots. 3 Mizuna Mustard seeds were planted into each of the 8 pots, 1 cm apart 
and around 0.5-1 cm deep. 
 
To make the positive control group, 100 mL of clay pellets was added to each of the eight 100 mL pots. 3 
Mizuna Mustard seeds were planted into individual clay pellets in each of the 8 pots. 
 
Direct Spherification: 
A 2% calcium chloride (CaCl2) bath to fill 800 mL of a 1000 mL beaker was created by combining 12.8 grams 
of CaCl2with 281.9 mL of water, then mixing until fully combined. In a separate mixture, 26.56g of Sodium 
Alginate, 4.8g Xanthan Gum, 281.9 mL distilled water, 1.152g of Osmocote Classic 14-14-14 fertilizer 
(Carolina Biological Supply), and 624g lunar regolith simulant were combined. 2 mL at a time of the regolith 
mixture was measured out, then placed into the CaCl2 bath for one minute. Next, they were removed, then left 
to sit for 1 minute before being rinsed with distilled water for another 1 minute. All of the spheres were 
removed from the water and placed into the dehydrator. Once they were dehydrated overnight, a small hole was 
poked in the center of 24 bubbles. In each bubble, a seed was placed inside, and finally, 8 wells were filled with 
Direct spheres, and 3 of the seed-containing bubbles were placed in each. 
 
Reverse Spherification: 
A 2% sodium alginate solution was prepared by mixing 26.56 g of sodium alginate with 800 mL of distilled 
water on a magnetic stirrer. In a separate mixture, 12.80g of CaCl2, 4.8g of Xanthan Gum, 281.9 mL of distilled 
water, 1.152g of Carolina Osmocote Classic fertilizer, and 624g of lunar regolith simulant were combined. 2mL 
of this was measured out at a time, then dropped into the sodium alginate solution and left for 1 minute. They 
were then removed and left to sit for another 1 minute. Then, they were rinsed with distilled water for 1 minute. 
All of the spheres were removed from the water and placed into the dehydrator. Once they were dehydrated 
overnight, a small hole was poked in the center of 24 bubbles. In each bubble, a seed was placed inside, and 
finally, 8 wells were filled with Reverse spheres, and 3 of the seed-containing bubbles were placed in each. 
 
 
Results 
Finalized plant growth was measured across the four experimental groups. Growth and health were evaluated by 
using the primary variables: shoot length, shoot-to-root ratio, and leaf count.

Plant Lengths per Group at Harvest. The 
average length after seven weeks of growth is 
measured in centimeters. Groups were measured 
separately and averaged. 
The average plant length in the final varied. The diameter had an average of 6.34 cm. Plant shoot length for the 
Positive Control had an average of 3.34 cm, with the Reverse group having 3.26 cm 
Graph 2: Line Graph Showcasing the Average 
Length of Shoots Each Week Over Time 
Average weekly shoot length for each group over 
7 weeks 
During the experiment, data on the shoot length of each group’s plants were also recorded weekly. It was 
tracked for 7 weeks of the 8-week growth period. Negative Control had no growth throughout the whole 
experiment. Reverse had a decline in week 4 but had an upward trend since then. Direct had a dip in shoot 
length in week 3, but had a rapid linear growth afterwards. Notably, Positive Control declined in weeks 3 and 4 
but gradually rose in length afterwards. 
Graph 3: Box Plot Showing the 
Root-to-Stem Ratio of Each Group 
The root-to-stem ratio was 
calculated by dividing the root 
length by the shoot length for each 
plant, represented by one dot

In addition to the shoot length, the ratio of shoot length to root length was calculated to show the amount of root 
allocation. A lower ratio indicates longer shoots than roots, therefore indicating less root allocation, healthier 
plants, and more nutrient availability. The Direct group had a ratio of 1.19. Reverse had a ratio of 1.23. The 
Positive Control Group showed a ratio of 1.79. The Negative Control had no growth in either the shoot or the 
root, so there is no ratio to be measured. 
 
 
Graph 4: Box Plot Showing the Biomass of Each Plant at Harvest 
Biomass was measured after seven weeks of growth. Each group was measured and averaged as a gram 
measurement. 
 
Furthermore, these growth patterns are mirrored in the plants’ biomass at harvest. Direct had an average 
biomass of .422 grams per plant and a sum of 8.443 grams. Subsequently, Positive Control has an average of 
.069 grams and a total of 1.033 grams. The Reverse group had an average biomass of .086 but a whole of .949 
grams. Since Negative Control had no growth, there was no biomass to weigh for this group. 
 
Graph 5: Line Graph of the Average Leaf Count for 
Each Group 
True leaves were counted on each plant after each 
week of the growth period. An average was taken for 
each group every week.

The number of leaves in each group was counted weekly to 
create an average number of leaves per plant for each group. 
The leaf count for Reverse initially decreased, then followed 
a linear trajectory until week 6, when it had 3.61 leaves, then 
it decreased again in week 7. The Positive Control increased 
slightly from week 1 to week 2, then increased significantly 
more the following week. Then it decreased again before 
decreasing again from week 6 to 7. Direct increased slightly 
leading up to week 2 before decreasing in week 3. After this, 
it increased considerably until week 6, where it reached 5.18 
leaves on average, then had a final decrease leading up to week 7. Negative Control showed no growth; there 
were no leaves either. 
 
 
 
Graph 6: Bar Chart Showing the Leaf Chlorophyll 
Content at Various Wavelengths 
Chlorophyll A and B were detected by extracting leaf 
pigments using 90% acetone and utilizing a 
spectrophotometer to measure Chlorophyll. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Graph 7: Bar Chart Showing the Total Chlorophyll Content per Group 
Raw data from the absorbance rates were taken to calculate the chlorophyll concentration in each group. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Chlorophyll concentration was taken as a cumulative average for each group when being measured. The 
absorbance was first measured using the wavelengths of 664 nm (nanometers) for Chlorophyll A and 644 nm 
for Chlorophyll B. The absorbance measured on average for all chlorophyll types was 1.8985 Absorbance Units 
(AU) for the Positive Control, 2.278 AU for the Direct group, and 2.4515 AU for the Reverse group. Using the 
measurements or averages, the numbers were plugged into an equation to find out the actual concentration of 
the chlorophyll. The Positive control had 6.56 µg/ml of chlorophyll, the Direct group had 8.37 µg/ml of 
chlorophyll, and the Reverse group had 7.07 µg/ml of chlorophyll.

Graph 8: Bar Chart Showcasing the 
Nitrogen Content in the Soil 
This data was taken using the 
Nitrogen Luster Leaf Rapitest 
capsule detector kit and lunar 
regolith companies with water used 
in the EB and Flow watering system. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Utilizing a pill soil test kit, the average concentration of nitrogen in each of the groups' soil was measured. The 
concentration of nitrogen was measured on a scale from 0 to 5, with 0 indicating little to no nitrogen and 5 
indicating a surplus of nitrogen in the soil. Sourced from the pill kit, a range of 2-3 is the most desired amount 
of nitrogen for plant growth. From the data collected, Positive Control and Reverse had a deficient amount of 
nitrogen in the soil, with a measurement of 1 from the kit. Conversely, the groups Negative Control and Direct 
had an adequate amount of nitrogen, with them scoring a 2. 
 
Analysis 
The data within the results section is analyzed based on growth, chlorophyll content, biomass, and nutrient 
measurements, and the methodology can be efficient depending on the data. The graphs and data presented 
represent the averages of plant growth over the last 7 weeks, which can be further applied and analyzed. 
 
Growth Analysis: 
The shoots were measured every week for 7 weeks, and had different averages for each group. The Negative 
Control had no growth over the 7 weeks and showed no progress, meaning the regolith, when kept as the 
control, did not support the growth of Mizuna Mustard. From Graph 1, some trends stood out, including a 
collective decrease in length in Week 3. This was due to the light being too harsh on the newly growing plants, 
causing them to yellow and wilt. The light was then changed, which could have altered the data in some form, 
but no qualitative or quantitative differences between the Midpoint growth date and final growth date were 
observed. As seen in Graph 3, the shoot to root ratio for Direct is much lower than that of the Positive Control 
group, showing adequate growth. The Reverse group, however, showed optimal growth rates when comparing 
the shoot to root growth ratio. The ratio for Reverse is the closest to the optimal plant growth ratio, being 1:5 or 
1:6 for root to shoot, respectively (Harris, 1992). Although the Reverse, Direct, Negative Control, and Positive 
Control groups showed no relative accuracy to the optimal growth ratio, the Reverse group presented the closest 
results. The results showed a different group to be sufficient for harvesting and consumption rather than for 
growth rate. With the data presented in Graph 2 of the results, it is seen that the shoot lengths between groups 
differ and would impact the rate of harvest and consumption. The Direct group showed a total growth of 145.7 
cm, which is 142.43% greater than the Positive Control. The next most growth was shown by the Positive 
Control group with 60.1 cm. The next largest growth was shown in the Reverse group with 39.1 cm, or 53.71% 
less than the Positive Control. The Negative Control had no germination; therefore, there were no shoot lengths

to measure. With all of the data in consideration, when it comes to harvesting, the shoot length and amount of 
leaves are important in comparison to the roots. This is because the roots will not be harvested or consumed. 
The results show that the shoots within the Direct group grew twice as much as both the Reverse and Positive 
Control groups. This demonstrates that the Direct group would be the most efficient with harvesting and 
consumption being the primary focuses during the growth period. The leaf count also presented similar relations 
to those in the shoot and root growth data. The number of leaves in each group was counted weekly to create an 
average of leaves a plant would have at the time taken. All groups showed a general increase in leaf count 
throughout the growth period. The Reverse group initially had the most leaves, but the average dropped 
significantly leading up to week 2 due to the initial harsh lighting and the loss of smaller true leaves. Although 
the plant length decreased for two of the groups during week 3, the leaf count increased on its normal trajectory 
during this time, except for the Direct group. Intriguingly, the Direct group was the only group that did not 
yellow during week 3. Throughout the growth period, Direct showed the highest count of leaves due to quick 
maturity. The next highest was the Positive Control, followed by the Reverse group. In the final week, all 
groups showed fewer leaves. This is mostly likely due to smaller leaves shriveling up, as bigger, stronger leaves 
grew and restricted light for them. The Positive Control had an average of 3.278 leaves, and the Reverse group 
had an average of 2.75 leaves. The Direct value showed the highest leaf count of 4.48. When considering the 
growth as per the null hypothesis, the sample values from the four groups were analyzed. With this sample data, 
a Tukey-Kramer ANOVA test was run on all sample data within the groups. The resulting p-value was 
0.00001106 regarding total plant growth, and the corresponding p-value regarding the number of leaves was 
0.0002643. This data from both total plant length and leaf count showed a significant difference between the 
Direct group and the positive control, as well as the Direct group and the Reverse group. However, the Reverse 
group data and Positive Control data did not show a significant difference. This allows for the conclusion that 
the null hypothesis was rejected, providing significant data 
 
Chlorophyll Analysis: 
The chlorophyll concentrations and absorption levels for each group provide results sufficient for analysis of 
which group is the healthiest and produces the most chlorophyll. The Reverse group experienced the highest 
amount of absorption, which was most likely due to the small but strong sample size, which was also clouded 
by material from the spheres. While looking at the concentrations, the ideal chlorophyll concentration of 12.6 
µg/mL was compared to the measured values (Flores et al 2024). This reference value would not be accurate, as 
there is no studied reference value for mizuna mustard grown in lunar soil. With the actual chlorophyll 
concentration, however, Reverse was deficient in comparison to the four groups. The group with deficient 
absorption and adequate chlorophyll was the Positive Control group, suggesting that the plants had a higher 
concentration of chlorophyll compared to the Reverse and would serve better for harvesting. However, results 
suggested that the Direct group would be best for harvest and growth based on the chlorophyll content and 
absorption. With adequate absorption and more than optimal chlorophyll concentration, the Direct group 
showed to be the best growth setup for growth, optimal chlorophyll, and future harvests. 
 
Biomass Analysis: 
The results from biomass collection were used to determine the quantity of growth rather than the quality of 
growth within the four groups. The four groups were compared, considering that the Negative Control had no 
growth, and the best group for harvest was determined. The results indicate varying biomasses for each group, 
but present the large difference within the Direct group, showing the largest amount of biomass, with this

measurement being 8.433 grams. This data suggests that when it came to the amount of growth, Direct was the 
most successful, therefore making it better for harvesting, getting maximum plant product, and observations. 
When observing the p-value of this test, it was concluded that it was 1.249e-8, determining the rejection of the 
null hypothesis, proving its significance. 
 
Nitrogen Analysis: 
The analyzed amounts for nitrogen determine how much nitrogen there is within the soil post-harvest, from a 
rating of N0 (Depleted) to N5 (Surplus). The Reverse and Positive Control groups had adequate amounts of 
nitrogen, while the Direct and Negative Control groups were almost deficient in nitrogen. The nitrogen likely 
varies between groups because of excess material such as the sodium alginate cover, the amount of nitrogen the 
plant took up, or the base amount of nitrogen when the soil was first implemented into the growth setup. The 
nitrogen levels could not be measured when first introduced in the growth setup, limiting the ability to persist if 
the nitrogen was taken up by the plants or the nitrogen was low when the experiment started. The plants in the 
Direct group likely used up the nitrogen in the soil, while the Reverse and control groups did not use much of 
the nitrogen within the growth medium. The low nitrogen levels in the Direct group were likely used to produce 
more chlorophyll (UCIPM, 2026), contrasting with the Reverse and control groups, which had higher levels of 
nitrogen not used up by the plants to make chlorophyll, complementing the data retrieved from chlorophyll 
collection. 
 
Conclusion 
The analysis presents two different conclusions for the experiment, one which answers the research questions, 
aims to reject or accept the null hypothesis, and is largely applicable to the issue identified in the introduction 
and background. The p-value within each group tested indicates that the data is statistically significant, leading 
to rejection of the null hypothesis; this was concluded in the p-values for both total plant growth and biomass. 
The data and analysis present the optimal growth, chlorophyll, nitrogen content, and harvest material from the 
group of Mizuna Mustard plants within the Direct spherification group. This goes against the initial hypothesis 
that the Reverse spherification group will produce the most optimal growth, even though the Reverse 
spherification group still performed better than the positive control. This indicates that spherification, especially 
Direct spherification, is a promising method of growing plants in lunar regolith that warrants further research. 
 
Having an intensive setup costs a significant amount of time. Future experiments should be completed with the 
preparation beforehand so that the entirety of the growth period can be utilized. An additional way of improving 
the quality of the results is to provide each tray with individual lights. Since only one light was available in the 
growth tent, trays received varying amounts of light, even though that one light was constantly set to the same 
light intensity every time it was on (except when the light intensity was permanently decreased during week 4 to 
mitigate plant damage).
